subject: Art & Design
title: Data Visualization: Making Numbers Visible
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Data Visualization: Making Numbers Visible.

hook.text: A table of 1,000 numbers is meaningless. A chart of those same numbers tells a story in seconds.

buildup.text: Bar charts compare quantities. Line charts show trends. Pie charts show proportions (badly, usually).

discovery.text: The secret to good data viz: remove everything that doesn't help the viewer understand the data faster.

twist.text: 3D charts, dual axes, and truncated scales are common tricks that distort data — intentionally or not.

climax.text: Edward Tufte's rule: maximize the data-ink ratio. Every drop of ink should represent data.

punchline.text: The best chart doesn't look impressive. It makes the data obvious.

quiz.question: What is Tufte's data-ink ratio principle?
options: Every element should represent data — remove non-data ink
Use as much color as possible

details.summary: Data visualization transforms raw numbers into visual patterns — bar charts, line graphs, heat maps, and scatter plots — that reveal trends, outliers, and relationships invisible in spreadsheets.
details.whyItMatters: Data drives decisions, and visualization determines how data is understood. Misleading charts can distort truth as effectively as false statements. Visual literacy in data is essential for informed citizenship.
takeaways: Visualization reveals patterns invisible in raw numbers
Charts, graphs, and maps make complex data accessible
Misleading visualization distorts truth as effectively as lies

faq.question: What makes a data visualization misleading?
faq.answer: Truncated Y-axes that exaggerate differences, cherry-picked time ranges, 3D effects that distort proportions, dual Y-axes with incompatible scales, and pie charts with too many slices. The most common trick is starting the Y-axis at a non-zero value to make small changes look dramatic.

faq.question: Which chart type should you use when?
faq.answer: Bar charts for comparisons, line charts for trends over time, scatter plots for correlations, pie charts for parts of a whole (5 or fewer slices), and heat maps for density. Choose the simplest type that communicates the data's story. If a simple bar chart works, don't use a complex infographic.
